t: Lecture Outline: The System of Regulatory Documents
n: In this lecture we will review the system of regulatory documents governing forensic chemical examination. In Uzbekistan, forensic medical examination is governed by the Law "On Forensic Examination". On the basis of the law, orders of the Ministry of Health were issued in 2011, 2012 and 2015. At the lower level are the standards for conducting forensic medical examinations and investigations, for example A-6. The hierarchy in the diagram is as follows: the law, Ministry orders and the instruction, forensic chemical rules, standards, and laboratory SOPs, that is, standard operating procedures.

On the adoption and structure of the law. The Legislative Chamber adopted it on 18 November 2009, and the Senate approved it on 7 May 2010. The Law "On Forensic Examination" consists of 5 chapters and 33 articles. The order of chapters is as follows: the first chapter covers general provisions, the second rights and duties, the third the conduct of examination, the fourth financing and support, and the fifth final provisions.

t: Structure of the Law: 5 Chapters and 33 Articles
n: Let us look at the structure of the law in more detail. The Law "On Forensic Examination" consists of 5 chapters and 33 articles. Chapter 1 covers general provisions; chapter 2, the rights and duties of the head of the institution and of the forensic expert; chapter 3, the conduct of examination. Chapter 4 covers financing, and the organisational, scientific-methodological and informational support of forensic expert activity; chapter 5, final provisions. In other words, each chapter of the law deals with a separate set of issues.

Article 3 defines the basic concepts of the law. A state forensic expert is a forensic expert who conducts examinations in the course of his or her official duties at a state forensic expert institution. A case means a civil, commercial or criminal case, pre-investigation inquiry materials, or an administrative offence case in which a forensic examination has been ordered. A forensic expert is a person with special knowledge in science, technology, art or a trade, appointed in the established manner and taking part in order to give an opinion. Forensic expert activity is the activity of organising and conducting forensic examinations.

The principles of activity are set out in Articles 4-8. The basic principles are given in Article 4; compliance with legality and with human rights is set out in Articles 5-6. Look at the table: Article 5, compliance with legality; Article 6, respect for human rights and freedoms; Article 7, independence of the forensic expert; Article 8, objectivity, comprehensiveness and completeness. The forensic expert is independent of the body that ordered the examination, of the parties, and of persons interested in the outcome of the case.

t: Map of the Articles of the Law: 12-24
n: Now the map of the articles of the law, Articles 12-24. Article 12, the state forensic expert institution; Articles 13-14, rights and duties of the head; Articles 15-16, rights and duties of the forensic expert. Article 17, grounds and time limits for conducting an examination; Article 18, additional and repeat examinations. Articles 19-21 define examination by a commission, and commission-based and complex examinations; Article 22, attendance of participants; Articles 23-24 are devoted to the opinion. Article 24 in the table concerns the impossibility of giving an opinion.

Article 9 is devoted to the objects of examination. The objects are: physical evidence, samples for examination, other material objects, corpses and their parts, and documents. Objects, except a living person, may be damaged or used up to the extent necessary for the examination. Where possible, objects are submitted wrapped and sealed; if they have not been used up completely, they are returned after the examination. In the diagram these objects are divided into five groups: physical evidence, samples for examination, other material objects, corpses and their parts, and documents.

t: The Forensic Expert: Requirements and Questioning (10-11)
n: The forensic expert and the requirements for the expert are covered in Articles 10-11. A state forensic expert, an employee of another organisation or another natural person may act as an expert. The expert is questioned only about the opinion given and the examinations personally conducted. Remember: questioning the expert before the opinion has been given is prohibited. A person with higher education who has completed training in a particular specialty is appointed to the post of state forensic expert; this is established in Article 11.

t: Rights and Duties of the Head of the Institution
n: Let us dwell on the rights and duties of the head of the institution. If there is no suitable specialist or material base, the head has the right to give notice of this without carrying out the order appointing the examination. The head explains to the expert his or her rights and duties and ensures the conditions necessary for the examination. When the examination is complete, the opinion, the objects and the case materials are sent to the body that ordered the examination. An important restriction: the head has no right to give the expert instructions that predetermine the course of the examination and the content of the conclusion.

t: Grounds and Time Limits for Conducting an Examination
n: Grounds and time limits for conducting an examination. The grounds for conducting an examination are the ruling of an inquirer, investigator, prosecutor or judge, and a court order. The examination is deemed ordered from the day the ruling or order is issued. The body that ordered the examination provides the objects and the case materials and obtains samples for examination. The examination is conducted within the time limits set by law. The sequence in the diagram is as follows: the ruling or order is issued, the examination is deemed ordered, the objects and materials are provided, and the examination is conducted on time.

Distinguish the types of examination. An additional examination is ordered to fill a gap, and a repeat examination if the opinion is unfounded or doubtful. A repeat examination is assigned to a different expert; the ruling states the reasons for disagreeing with the previous opinion. In a commission-based examination, several experts of the same specialty take part, and in a complex examination, experts of different specialties. If disagreements arise, each member of the commission gives a separate opinion.

The expert's opinion is regulated by Articles 23-24. The opinion is certified by the signature of the expert or, in a commission examination, of each member of the commission. The opinion states the date and place, the grounds, the expert's details, the questions, the objects, the methods used, the assessment of the results, and reasoned answers. If the question cannot be resolved or the object is unsuitable, a document on the impossibility of giving an opinion is drawn up. When the examination is complete, the opinion, the objects and the case materials are sent to the body that ordered the examination.

The last articles of the law, from Article 25 to Article 33. They cover financing, organisational and scientific-methodological support, informational support, protection and international cooperation. Also covered here are remuneration and social protection of state experts, liability for violating the law, and entry into force. An important fact: state forensic expert institutions are financed from the state budget. That is, the activity of the institutions is financially provided for by the state, which also serves the independence of experts.

t: Map of the Articles of the Law: 25-33
n: We continue the map of the articles, 25-33. Article 25, financing of forensic expert activity; Article 26, organisational and scientific-methodological support; Article 27, informational support. Article 28, protection of state forensic expert institutions; Article 29, international cooperation; Article 30, remuneration and social protection of experts. Article 31, liability for violating legislation; Article 32, coordination; Article 33, entry of the law into force. In the table they are grouped: 26-27, scientific-methodological and informational support; 28, protection of institutions; 29, international cooperation; 30, remuneration and social protection; 31-33, liability and entry into force.

Now the ministry instruction, that is, the instruction of the Ministry of Health, 2011. The instruction was approved by order of the Ministry of Health dated 25 July 2011. It was registered with the Ministry of Justice on 2 September 2011 under number 2259 and entered into force on 12 September 2011. The instruction is based on the law and on the Criminal Procedure and Civil Procedure Codes. Remember the dates in sequence: the order, registration, entry into force.

t: The Instruction: Types of Examination and Time Limits
n: The instruction sets out the types of examination and the time limits. The types of examination are: of corpses, of living persons, of physical evidence and biological objects, including forensic chemical and chemical-toxicological examination. Time limits for conducting an examination are set within thirty days, depending on complexity. If it cannot be completed in thirty days, the head draws up a reasoned opinion three days before the deadline expires. The period is counted from the day after the materials are received.

Orders and the Presidential Resolution. Examination is conducted on the basis of the Ministry of Health orders of 2011, 2012 and 2015. In the table: the order of 25 July 2011; the order of 1 July 2012, No. 153; the order of 15 April 2015, No. 82; the Presidential Resolution of 4 December 2018, PP-4049. By this resolution the Main Bureau was transformed into the Republican Scientific and Practical Centre. The bureaux of the regions and of the city of Tashkent were reorganised as branches of the Centre.

The structure of the forensic chemical rules. The rules are given as Appendix 6 to the Ministry of Health order; this is a draft text in which the date and number are not indicated. The rules were drawn up by the head of the Main Bureau, Prof. Z.A. Giyosov, and the head of the forensic chemistry department, I.G. Akhmedjanov. The rules consist of 5 sections: general provisions, reception and description, conduct of the examination, formalisation of results, and storage of documents and evidence. The order in the diagram is the same: first general provisions, then reception, then the examination, formalisation of results and, finally, storage. This order covers the whole course of forensic chemical work.

The rules define the tasks of forensic chemical investigation. The first task: to detect and quantify toxicologically significant substances in order to establish the cause of death. The second: to detect, quantify and interpret the results for narcotic, psychotropic and medicinal substances isolated from biological material. The third: qualitative and quantitative analysis of non-biological evidence submitted together with biological objects, that is, a liquid, ampoule, tablet or powder. The quantity of the objects must be sufficient for the investigation and for possible repeat analysis.

The requirements of the rules concerning premises, safety and the archive. The examination is conducted in rooms with ventilation, a fume cupboard, gas, water, heating, earthed electrical wiring and good natural light. The forensic chemistry department is separated from other departments; when work is finished it is locked and sealed. Objects from infected persons, that is, in tuberculosis, hepatitis or AIDS, are sent in a special container. Examination of volatile and perishable substances begins on the day of receipt. Two thirds of a physical evidence object is used for analysis, and one third is kept in the department archive for repeat analysis; this is established in paragraph 9.

t: Rules: Plan and Purity of Reagents
n: On the plan and the purity of reagents. Before the investigation, the expert becomes familiar with the documents and draws up an investigation plan. If the document states a purpose, the investigation is carried out only for the substances stated in the document. Reagents, vessels and instruments must be chemically pure; the purity of a reagent is checked with the very method and reaction in which it is used. Wherever possible, at least two methods based on different physical or chemical principles are applied.

The methods are divided into two groups. Preliminary methods: colour reactions, thin-layer chromatography and enzyme immunoassay methods. Confirmatory methods: spectrophotometry in the UV, visible and IR regions, atomic absorption, GLC, HPLC, and chromatography-mass spectrometry. The quantity is expressed in units of weight per 100 g of the object; at least two determinations are carried out on each object. That is, the preliminary method gives a presumption, and the confirmatory method confirms it.

t: Rules: Repeat and Additional Investigation, Quality
n: We distinguish between repeat and additional investigation. In a repeat investigation, all the investigations carried out in the primary one are performed, as well as those not carried out. In an additional investigation, only the investigations not carried out previously are performed. Internal laboratory and external quality control, directed at the method and the substance, is carried out. In a full analysis, a conversion coefficient is applied to account for the expert's work; this is a conventional unit of calculation. Remember the difference: a repeat investigation fully repeats and also performs what was missing, whereas an additional investigation only supplements what was not done.

Formalising the results. The result of the examination is formalised as an "expert opinion", and the result of the investigation as a "forensic chemical investigation report". The opinion, that is, the report, consists of three parts: introductory, investigative and concluding. The introduction states the time, grounds, place, expert, objects and case, the purpose and questions, and the "Circumstances of the case". The investigative part includes the "Description of the objects" and the "Chemical investigation"; if necessary, microscopic examination is also recorded.

t: Recording the Chemical Investigation and the Conclusion
n: Rules for recording the chemical investigation and the conclusion. For each operation, the quantity of the object taken is stated; the isolation methods and the observed phenomena are described in full. In the report it is not permitted to write the expressions "positive" or "negative reaction", the name of the author of a method, or the formulae and equations of reactions. In the conclusion, first the substances found are given with their quantities, then the substances not found, and finally the answers to the questions.

t: Storage of Documents and Physical Evidence
n: Rules for storing documents and physical evidence. Case documents are kept in a separate folder and, once work is finished, in a sealable safe or a lockable cabinet. Physical evidence is kept in a separate lockable, sealable cabinet; perishable objects are kept in a locked and sealed refrigerator. Evidence liable to putrefaction, if it cannot be returned, is preserved in ethyl alcohol and kept in the refrigerator for one year. Objects submitted for the determination of ethyl alcohol are destroyed 30 days after the investigation is complete.

On the standards of forensic medical examination. The standards were developed on the basis of legislative norms and the "procedure for conducting forensic medical examination" and are intended for all institutions. The aims are to improve activity, to ensure the objectivity of expert opinions, and to make accreditation by international organisations possible. The standard code consists of a letter and a number. The letter A denotes examination of a corpse, V living persons, S repeat, commission-based and complex examination, B forensic biological, Ye forensic histological, and G‘ medico-criminalistic examination.

Standard A-6 defines the taking of objects for forensic chemical investigation. The type of objects is chosen taking into account the nature of the suspected poison, its route of administration, distribution, rate of elimination and therapeutic measures. It is taken into account that one third of the internal organs and fluids remains in the archive for repeat examination. When poisoning is suspected, the following are taken: stomach contents, 1/3 of the liver, bile, one kidney, urine up to 200 ml and 200 ml of blood; each is placed in a separate glass jar.

t: A-6: Additional Objects by Route of Administration
n: Under A-6, additional objects are taken depending on the route of administration. If the poison is suspected to have been introduced through the vagina or uterus, the vagina and uterus are taken in separate glass vessels. For subcutaneous or intramuscular administration, skin and muscle are taken from the area of suspected administration. In inhalation poisoning, 300 g each of a lung portion from the most blood-filled area and the brain are taken. If particles, crystals or tablets are found in the stomach contents, they too are sent for examination.

Under A-6, objects according to substance, part one. When ethanol is suspected, blood is taken from large veins or from the sinuses of the dura mater. In the table, for ethanol, blood and urine 10-20 ml, filled to the stopper. For narcotic and psychotropic substances, blood 150 ml, urine 150-200 ml and the gallbladder are taken. For carbon monoxide, blood 10-20 ml. If blood and urine have not been submitted, about 100 g of muscle tissue is submitted. For acids and alkalis, the larynx, trachea, oesophagus, stomach wall and a piece of skin are taken.

Under A-6, objects according to substance, part two. For methyl alcohol, brain, liver and kidney 100 g each are taken, as well as blood and urine. For volatile organochlorine substances, a piece of omentum, 200 g of brain, blood, urine, liver and kidney are taken. For glycosides, tissues of the injection area are taken preserved in ethyl alcohol. For organophosphorus compounds, liver, kidney, urine, stomach, intestine and blood for cholinesterase activity are taken.

Metallic poisons, methaemoglobin and exhumation. In mercury poisoning and in chronic lead, thallium and arsenic poisoning, hair and nails are also taken. For poisons that form methaemoglobin, for example aniline and nitrobenzene, blood is taken. In the table, for mushrooms and poisonous plants, gastrointestinal contents and vomit are indicated. In exhumation, 500 g of soil from each of six places, as well as clothing and a board of the coffin, are submitted.

t: A-6: Volumes of the Main Objects
n: Let us summarise the volumes of the main objects under A-6. When ethanol is suspected, blood and urine are taken, 10-20 ml each, in a vessel filled to the stopper. When narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances are suspected, blood 150 ml, urine 150-200 ml and the gallbladder are always taken. When methyl alcohol is suspected, brain, liver and kidney 100 g each are taken; blood and urine 10-20 ml each. When carbon monoxide is suspected, blood 10-20 ml is taken. In general poisoning, blood is taken in the amount of 200 ml.

t: A-6: Rules for Taking and Preservation
n: Rules for taking and preservation under A-6. So that the contents of the oesophagus, stomach and intestine do not mix, two ligatures are applied; internal organs are not washed with water. Organs are placed in dry wide-mouthed glass jars; the use of metal or ceramic vessels is prohibited. Preservation is carried out only when cardiac glycosides are suspected: ethyl alcohol must cover the organs by at least 1 cm, and 300 ml of alcohol is submitted as a sample. The jars are closed tightly, a label is attached, and they are placed in a sealed polyethylene bag or container.

t: A-6: Expert Supervision and Preparing Vessels
n: Expert supervision and preparation of vessels under A-6. The expert ensures that the poison does not escape from the corpse and does not get in from outside. Before the corpse is opened, the autopsy table, instruments and gloves are washed thoroughly; during the examination, water and other liquids are not used. The jars are washed with a soda or mustard solution, rinsed with clean water and then with distilled water, and dried in a drying cabinet. The procedure has four stages: solution, clean water, distilled water, drying.

About laboratory SOPs. An SOP is a "procedure instruction"; for example, No. RIP.G.240.2013 is for determining mercury in biological material. Another SOP, No. RIP.G.244.2013, is for determining carboxyhaemoglobin in blood. The document is approved by the Main Bureau; the compilers are named; staff sign the familiarisation sheet. The sections of an SOP are: materials, prepared reagents, description of the procedure, and analysis, interpretation and documentation. According to the table, the description of the procedure gives the method step by step, and the analysis, interpretation and documentation section sets out the result and the acceptance criteria.

Reagents and acceptance criteria in an SOP. The steps for preparing reagents are written down and the shelf life is stated: most 1 month, dithizone solution 10 days, copper(I) iodide 6 months. The acceptance criterion for mercury: the reagents used and the control sample must not give a positive reaction for mercury. The acceptance criterion for carboxyhaemoglobin: work is done under conditions of minimal contact of the blood with air; for photometry the blood solutions must be clear.

Let us conclude the topic. The hierarchy of documents: the law, then Ministry orders and the instruction, the rules, standards and SOPs. The law consists of 5 chapters and 33 articles; the basic principles are legality, independence, objectivity and completeness. Standard A-6: objects are taken according to the type of poison; one third remains in the archive. Review questions: the structure of the law, the rights and duties of the expert, object volumes under A-6, and the sections of an SOP.
